title: Building a Truthful Resume
summary: Learn how to build a clear, truthful resume that presents your education, experience, skills, projects, and accomplishments without exaggerating qualifications or claiming evidence you do not have.
objectives: Identify the major sections of a basic resume.
Write accurate descriptions of experience and accomplishments.
Distinguish truthful presentation from exaggeration or unsupported claims.

vocab.def: A concise document that summarizes relevant education, experience, skills, projects, and accomplishments.
A short statement describing relevant strengths, interests, preparation, and goals.
A result, contribution, improvement, or completed piece of work that can be described accurately.
Information or work that supports a claim about what you completed, produced, demonstrated, or achieved.

sections.heading: A resume is a professional summary, not a life story
sections.body: A strong resume focuses on information relevant to the opportunity. Common sections include contact information, summary, education, experience, projects, skills, credentials actually earned, and selected accomplishments.

sections.heading: Describe what you actually did
sections.body: Use specific language about tasks, projects, responsibilities, tools, teamwork, and results. Avoid claiming authority, credentials, job titles, or outcomes that you did not actually have.

sections.heading: Projects and learning experiences can count
sections.body: Students may not yet have long employment histories. School projects, community work, volunteering, structured training, supervised practice, and evidence-backed projects can still demonstrate useful experience.

sections.heading: Truthful language builds trust
sections.body: If you completed preparation but not an external credential, say that accurately. If you contributed to a team project, describe your contribution rather than taking credit for the whole team's work.

practice.prompt: You completed a course about data center operations but have never worked in a data center. Which resume statement is stronger?
practice.answer: Describe the course, projects, simulations, or skills practiced rather than claiming professional data center employment.

practice.prompt: Your team built a project and you were responsible for testing and documentation. Should your resume say you built the entire project alone?
practice.answer: No. Describe your actual testing and documentation contributions accurately.

quiz.question: Which resume statement is strongest?
options: A specific, truthful description of what you actually did and can support
The most impressive claim even if it is exaggerated
A credential you plan to earn later
A job title you never held
quiz.answer: A specific, truthful description of what you actually did and can support

lab.objective: Draft a one-page student resume using simulated or learner-selected education, experience, projects, skills, and accomplishments while separating verified facts from unsupported claims.

reflectionPrompt: Why can an accurate description of a smaller accomplishment be stronger than an exaggerated claim?
